summary: This proposed standard presents requirements for deploying NFSv4 to build a single file namespace across environments with multiple NFSv4 domains. A participating server must offer a multi-domain-capable file system and support RPCSEC_GSS for user authentication.

eli5.summary: Different organizations might want to share one big folder tree. This lists what their file servers must support so people from each side are recognized and kept safe.

questions: can auth_sys be used in a multi-domain nfsv4 deployment
what are stringified uid and gid
subtitle: What an NFSv4 deployment must do before several organizations can share one file namespace.

tldr.problem: NFSv4 lets each NFSv4 Domain choose its own way of naming users, but a namespace spanning several domains needs identities that never collide.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets deployment requirements: unique name@domain identities, RPCSEC_GSS authentication with cross-domain trust, no AUTH_SYS or stringified UID/GIDs, and multi-domain-capable file systems.
tldr.outcome: Stand-alone setups that rely on AUTH_SYS or stringified IDs cannot join a multi-domain namespace, while an RPCSEC_GSS setup with name@domain can if it meets a short list of conditions.

today: RFC 8000 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Multi-Domain Needs Rules
sections.content:
NFSv4 introduced the NFSv4 Domain: a set of users and groups that use the name@domain syntax with the same @domain part. Earlier NFS versions such as NFSv3 (RFC 1813) used numeric user and group IDs, which are not unique across deployments and so do not scale to many naming domains.

NFSv4 also has a referral mechanism that lets one server or a set of servers present a namespace spread across file systems on multiple servers. Together with name@domain and RPCSEC_GSS security, this makes a multi-domain file namespace possible.

This document lists requirements for such deployments. In short, a participating server must offer a multi-domain-capable file system and support RPCSEC_GSS for user authentication, and in most cases it must also support identity-mapping services.
sections.eli5: Numbers like 'student 1001' work inside one school but clash when schools merge. Names with a school attached, like sam@northschool, stay different.

sections.title: Key Terms and the Federated File System
sections.content:
The RFC defines a stand-alone NFSv4 Domain as a deployment with a single NFSv4 Domain. A local representation of identity is what a file system stores on disk, such as a numeric UID or GID or a Windows SID. A unique identity is an on-the-wire form that is unique across the whole multi-domain namespace, for example name@domain or a Kerberos principal. A stringified UID or GID is an owner or group string made of decimal digits with no leading zeros and no @ sign.

The Federated File System (FedFS, RFC 5716) is the standardized way to build an enterprise-wide NFSv4 namespace. The requirements here apply to all multi-domain deployments, whether or not they run as a FedFS. Some stand-alone configurations are not compatible with joining a multi-domain FedFS.

The word 'domain' means several things in this area: a DNS domain, a security realm, a FedFS domain and an administrative domain. In this document 'multi-domain' always means multiple NFSv4 Domains.
sections.eli5: The same word, 'domain', is used for several different things, like how 'club' can mean a golf club or a sandwich. The RFC says exactly which meaning it uses.

sections.title: Identity Mapping on Servers and Clients
sections.content:
NFSv4 servers deal with authentication identities (principals) and authorization identities (users and groups). Depending on what is sent on the wire and what is stored on disk, a server may need two mappings: auth-to-authz, from the authentication identity to authorization context such as group memberships, and wire-to-disk, from the on-the-wire identity to the on-disk representation. A name service such as LDAP often provides both. Servers use them for file access decisions and for setting or listing metadata such as ACLs or permissions.

Clients need mapping too. Client APIs usually express identity in a local form such as a UNIX UID/GID, so when stringified IDs cannot be used, the client must convert between that local form and a unique identity when setting or reading owner and group attributes. The need would not arise if clients could use the unique representation directly.
sections.eli5: Inside the computer, people are numbers, but on the network they are names with a school attached. Someone has to translate between the two, like a receptionist with a directory.

sections.title: Stand-Alone Deployment Examples
sections.content:
The RFC walks through three stand-alone setups for a server exporting a POSIX UID/GID-based file system, in order of increasing administrative complexity.

  • AUTH_SYS with stringified UID/GID. The closest NFSv4 gets to NFSv3. The RPC credential carries a UID and a list of GIDs, so file access needs no name service, and metadata listing needs none either because the ID can be rebuilt from the string.
  • AUTH_SYS with name@domain. File access is the same, but metadata setting and listing needs a name service for the wire-to-disk mapping, often through nsswitch.
  • RPCSEC_GSS with name@domain. Typically Kerberos 5 is used, with principals like principal@REALM. Authorization context cannot always be counted on to arrive with authentication, so file access needs both a wire-to-disk mapping and an auth-to-authz mapping.
sections.eli5: There are three ways a single school can run its login desk, from just checking a number to checking a name against a proper ID card. Only the last one is strong enough when many schools share.

sections.title: Multi-Domain Constraints
sections.content:
Joining domains under one namespace costs some administrative freedom. For name@domain, the domain part MUST be unique within the multi-domain namespace and the name part MUST be unique within its NFSv4 Domain. Because UIDs and GIDs collide between domains, stringified UID/GIDs MUST NOT be used, and multi-domain-capable servers MUST reject requests that use them.

The NFSv4 Domain name is loosely defined as a DNS domain name, which is a good fit because DNS names are globally unique. One NFSv4 Domain may span several DNS domains (one name is chosen), and several NFSv4 Domains may share a DNS domain, but only one of them can use the DNS name itself. Each NFSv4 Domain needs a single name resolution service able to convert its names to the local representation.

On security, the RPCSEC_GSS mechanism used is REQUIRED to have a method of cross-domain trust, so a principal from one domain can be authenticated in another. Kerberos is an example. AUTH_NONE can grant universal read-only access to public data. AUTH_SYS MUST NOT be used in a multi-domain deployment, because it carries bare numeric IDs with no domain and no namespace negotiation, so collisions can occur when more than one name service is involved.
sections.eli5: Every school needs a different name, and every kid in a school needs a different name. Kids must show a real ID card, not just say a number, and the same school-wide ID system has to be trusted by the other schools.

sections.title: Who Can Join and How Authorization Is Resolved
sections.content:
Revisiting the three examples: all would need to export multi-domain-capable file systems. The first (AUTH_SYS with stringified IDs) cannot join. The second uses name@domain but AUTH_SYS rules it out. The third (RPCSEC_GSS with name@domain) can join if its domain name is unique across the namespace, all exported file systems are multi-domain capable, and a secure method is used to resolve the remote principal's authorization information from an authoritative source.

Section 8 says a server SHOULD obtain that authorization context securely from an authoritative source, such as the name service of the principal's own domain. It lists three general methods and leaves the details out of scope:

  1. A mechanism-specific GSS-API authorization payload, such as a privilege attribute certificate (PAC) or principal authorization data (PAD). This is the preferred method.
  2. A local name service made authoritative for the remote domain through a security agreement and regular update feeds.
  3. An authenticated direct query to the principal's own domain name service.
sections.eli5: Only the school with proper ID cards can join the big library. When a visiting kid shows up, the librarian checks with the kid's own school, or reads the details printed on the card.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it discusses security throughout, since the requirements above are mostly about authentication and identity. It adds that all the security considerations of the relevant protocols apply, including NFSv4.0 (RFC 7530), NFSv4.1 (RFC 5661), RPCSEC_GSS (RFC 2203), GSS-API (RFC 4121), LDAP (RFC 4511) and the FedFS documents.
sections.eli5: The safety rules are built into the whole list, and the safety rules of every tool used along the way still apply too.

cells: AUTH_SYS and stringified IDs are not allowed
Needs a unique domain name, multi-domain-capable file systems and secure resolution of remote authorization data
